corpus_definition: a person learning a skill by working with an expert

forms.definition: a young person who learns a job by working with an expert
forms.example: He started as an apprentice to a skilled carpenter.

syn.note: Very close; a trainee can learn any job, often in an office or company.
Easy, general word for anyone who is learning something.
An intern works for a short time, often a student in an office; an apprentice learns a craft for years.
Easy word for someone who has just started; it does not mean working with an expert.

ant.note: The skilled worker who teaches the learner: a master carpenter.
A person with a lot of skill and knowledge.

forms.definition: a period of time when you learn a job from an expert
forms.example: His apprenticeship at the bakery lasted three years.

syn.note: General word for learning the skills for a job.
Usually shorter and in an office; often for students.

forms.definition: to send someone to learn a craft by working with an expert
forms.example: At sixteen, he was apprenticed to a tailor in Bukhara.
forms.note: Usually passive: be apprenticed to someone. Not common in everyday English.

syn.note: General word for teaching someone the skills for a job.

forms.note: No adjective. Use the noun before another noun: an apprentice electrician.

context.text: My cousin is an apprentice in a car workshop in Samarkand. His apprenticeship lasts two years, and then he hopes to open his own garage.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); verb is a rare conversion, usually passive.

corpus_definition: To think that something is right or good.
particle_note: Not separable: 'approve of my friends', never 'approve my friends of'. Patterns: approve of + noun / -ing; approve of someone doing something.

relations.note: Easy word; like is about enjoying, approve of is about thinking something is right.
You agree with an idea and help it happen.
Close: you think an idea or action is right.
Weaker: you allow it, but you may not think it is good.
To think that something is wrong or bad.
To say that you do not like or agree with something.

context.text: My grandmother doesn't approve of eating in front of the TV. But she approves of my plan to study medicine in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Different from 'approve' without 'of' (officially accept a plan); this map covers the opinion sense only.

corpus_definition: to begin to happen or exist; to come up as a new issue

forms.note: No noun in this family. Use 'occurrence' or 'appearance' instead.

forms.definition: to begin to happen, often as a problem or question
forms.example: Problems arose when the project lost its funding.
forms.note: Irregular: arise, arose, arisen. Don't confuse with rise (go up) and raise (lift something).

syn.note: Everyday English with the same meaning: 'A problem came up.'
Formal word for happen.
Easy, general word; arise is used most for problems and questions.
Used when something becomes known: 'New facts emerged.'
Informal; used when something appears suddenly.

ant.note: To stop existing or go away.

context.text: If any questions arise during the exam, raise your hand. Last year a problem arose with the computers, so the test started late.

reviewer_note: Rise and raise look similar but are separate words, listed as not_family; no false a- prefix claimed.

corpus_definition: The study of numbers and basic ****** to combine them.

forms.definition: the part of maths that uses adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing
forms.example: We practiced arithmetic in math class today.
forms.note: Also means a calculation: 'Let me check your arithmetic.'

syn.note: The act of working out a number.
Maths (British) or math (American) is the whole subject; arithmetic is only the basic part.
British, informal: 'do sums' = do simple arithmetic.
The ability to work with numbers.

forms.definition: connected with adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing numbers
forms.example: The test checks basic arithmetical skills.

syn.note: Wider: about all of maths, not only simple sums.
Connected with numbers in general.

forms.definition: connected with simple calculations with numbers
forms.example: An arithmetic mistake made the final answer wrong.
forms.note: Same spelling as the noun, used before another noun.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with simple calculations
forms.example: The answer is arithmetically correct, but the method is wrong.

syn.note: Wider: connected with maths in general.
In a way connected with numbers.

context.text: My little brother is good at arithmetic, but he made one arithmetical mistake in his homework. The teacher said his answer was arithmetically wrong but well explained.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: definition has a masked word ('******', probably 'operations'); copied as given. Adjective has two real forms: arithmetical and the conversion arithmetic.

forms.definition: the quality of not being natural or real
forms.example: Critics noticed the artificiality of the film's happy ending.

syn.note: The quality of not being true or real.

forms.note: No verb. The old word 'artifice' (a clever trick) is rare and literary.

forms.definition: made by people, not by nature; not real
forms.example: These flowers are made of artificial silk.

syn.note: Made by people; very close.
Easy word; fake often means made to trick people.
Made from chemicals, for example fabrics or materials.
Not real or not true: false teeth.

ant.note: Made by nature, not by people.
Easy word: the true thing, not a copy.
Really what it seems to be.

forms.definition: in a way that is made or done by people, not nature
forms.example: The fruit was artificially coloured to look fresher.

syn.note: In a way that is not normal or natural.

ant.note: In a natural way, without help from people.

context.text: My aunt never uses artificial flowers in her house in Fergana. She says fruit that is artificially sweetened tastes strange too.

reviewer_note: artifice is related by origin but rare; mentioned only in a note. artificial intelligence (AI) is a compound phrase, left out.

corpus_definition: The grey powder left after something has burned.

forms.definition: the grey powder that is left after a fire
forms.example: The fire left only ash in the fireplace.
forms.note: Plural 'ashes' is used for what is left of a fire or of a dead body. Ash is also a kind of tree (another meaning).

syn.note: Small pieces of burned wood or coal that are not fully powder.
Black powder from smoke, found inside chimneys.
Pieces of wood still hot and glowing after a fire.
Easy word for any fine dry powder.

forms.definition: very pale in the face because of shock or illness
forms.example: Her face was ashen when she heard the news.
forms.note: Belongs to ash = a pale grey colour, used about faces; not the powder from a fire.

context.text: After the picnic in the mountains, we put water on the fire. Only grey ash was left, and the wind blew it across the grass.

reviewer_note: Only one existing form; ashtray is a compound (left out); ashen kept as other_meaning (face colour).

corpus_definition: feeling bad because you did something wrong
usage_note: be/feel ashamed of + noun / -ing / yourself: 'He was ashamed of his behavior.' Also: ashamed that + clause; ashamed to + verb. Not used before a noun: say 'an ashamed boy' rarely; prefer 'the boy was ashamed'.

relations.note: Embarrassed is about feeling silly in front of others; ashamed is about feeling you did something wrong.
Guilty is knowing you did wrong; ashamed adds a feeling that others think less of you.
Easy word; you feel bad and wish you had not done it.
Much stronger: made to look stupid in public.
Feeling happy about something you or someone close to you did.

context.text: Bobur was ashamed of shouting at his little sister. He said sorry, and now he is proud of how kind he is to her.

reviewer_note: Fixed adjective + preposition phrase; noun shame is not listed because phrases have no forms.

corpus_definition: To put together all the parts of a piece of equipment.

forms.definition: the process of putting the parts of something together
forms.example: The furniture is cheaper, but assembly is not included.
forms.note: Also means a large meeting of people, a different meaning.

syn.note: The process of building something, often a large thing like a house.
Easy word for making something by joining parts.
Making goods in large numbers in a factory.

forms.definition: to join all the parts of something together
forms.example: It is easy to assemble this new chair.

syn.note: Everyday English with the same meaning.
Easy word; build is also used for houses and roads.
Formal; often for large things like bridges.
To get equipment ready to use, not only to join its parts.

ant.note: To separate something into its parts.
Formal: to take a machine or structure apart.
Technical: to take apart, the exact opposite.

forms.definition: with all the parts already joined together
forms.example: The bike arrives fully assembled and ready to ride.

syn.note: Made by joining parts.

people.definition: a person or machine that puts the parts of products together
people.example: She works as an assembler in a car factory near Andijan.

context.text: My father assembled the new bookshelf on Saturday. Assembly took three hours because the instructions were in Chinese.

reviewer_note: assembly here = putting parts together; the meeting sense is its own map (headword assembly). disassemble listed as antonym, not a form (rule 3).

corpus_definition: A large group of people meeting in one place for a reason.

forms.definition: a large group of people who meet in one place for a reason
forms.example: The school held an assembly in the main hall.
forms.note: Also the name for some groups that make laws, and for putting parts together (another meaning).

syn.note: A group of people who come together; very close.
Easy word; a meeting can be small, an assembly is usually large.
People gathered in a mosque or church for prayer.
A large public meeting to support a cause or person.
Many people together, but not organised for a meeting.

forms.definition: to come together in one place as a group
forms.example: All the students assembled in the yard before the ceremony.

syn.note: Very close and more common.
Easy everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Easy word; meet is used for groups of any size.
Formal: used for official meetings.

ant.note: When a crowd goes away in different directions.
To move quickly in many different directions.

forms.definition: gathered together in one place
forms.example: The director thanked the assembled guests for coming.
forms.note: Usually after 'the' and before a noun: the assembled crowd.

syn.note: Very close and a little less formal.

context.text: Every Monday our school has an assembly. All the classes assemble in the hall, and the headteacher speaks to the assembled pupils about the week.

reviewer_note: Meeting sense only; the building sense (putting parts together) is covered by the separate assemble map.

corpus_definition: To help someone do a task.

forms.definition: help that you give to someone
forms.example: Please call this number if you need any assistance.

syn.note: Everyday word with the same meaning.
Often help with money, food or medicine: foreign aid.
Help and encouragement, often over a long time.

ant.note: Something that makes a task harder.

forms.definition: in sport, a pass that helps a teammate score
forms.example: He scored one goal and made two assists.
forms.note: Belongs to the sports meaning (football, basketball), not general help.

forms.definition: to help someone do a job or task
forms.example: Can you assist me with these boxes?

syn.note: Everyday word; assist is more formal.
Formal; often used in writing.
Help, often by giving money, advice or encouragement.
To support someone, often by agreeing with them.

ant.note: To make it harder for someone to do something.
Formal: to block or stop progress.

forms.definition: designed to help people with a disability do things
forms.example: Assistive technology helps blind students read on computers.
forms.note: Mostly used in 'assistive technology' and 'assistive devices'.

syn.note: Easy, general word for giving help.
Usually about people who give kindness and encouragement.

people.definition: a person whose job is to help another person in their work
people.example: The doctor's assistant took my blood pressure.

context.text: My sister works as an assistant in a clinic in Namangan. She assists the doctor every morning, and patients often ask her for assistance with forms.

reviewer_note: Sports noun 'an assist' kept as other_meaning; assistant goes in people (rule 8).
